content: Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) are a group of bacteria that are commonly found in soil, dust, and water. These bacteria are distinct from Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which causes tuberculosis, and Mycobacterium leprae, which causes Hansen’s disease (leprosy). While anyone can develop an NTM infection, individuals with pre-existing lung diseases or weakened immune systems are at a higher risk. There are over 190 recognized species of NTM, and some of these species are capable of causing disease in humans. The symptoms of an NTM infection vary depending on the site of infection but may include coughing, blood in the sputum, shortness of breath, fever, night sweats, weight loss, decreased appetite, loss of energy, and skin rashes. NTM infections most commonly affect the lungs, but they can also involve the skin and soft tissues (often following surgery, trauma, or injections), lymph nodes (especially in children), areas of the body with medical devices, and sterile sites such as the bloodstream (more common in individuals with compromised immune systems or those who have undergone invasive medical procedures). Exposure to NTM can occur through contact with contaminated water sources, including natural bodies of water (like rivers and streams), municipal water supplies, showerheads, sink faucets, hydrotherapy equipment (e.g., jetted therapy baths), ice machines, and decorative water features. Certain environments, such as tattoo parlors, nail salons, hot tubs, spas, and healthcare settings, may pose an increased risk of exposure. Outbreaks of NTM infections in healthcare settings typically occur when contaminated water is introduced during medical procedures. NTM bacteria can survive in moist environments, such as the interior of water pipes. When contaminated water is aerosolized, such as through the steam from a shower or a hot tub, individuals may inhale the bacteria, leading to infection. NTM infections can also occur at surgical or injection sites. However, NTM infections are not typically transmitted from person to person. Individuals with pre-existing lung conditions, such as cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, or emphysema, are particularly vulnerable to lung infections caused by NTM. People with weakened immune systems are also at higher risk of developing infections in other parts of the body. Preventing NTM infections requires effective water management programs, particularly in healthcare facilities, to reduce the risk of healthcare-associated infections. Public health departments play a critical role in supporting prevention efforts and responding to outbreaks. Treatment of NTM infections is often complex and requires consultation with specialists in infectious diseases or pulmonary medicine. NTM bacteria are resistant to many antibiotics, making treatment challenging. Therapy typically involves a combination of two to three antibiotics taken for six months to a year or longer, depending on the severity and location of the infection. One related condition is caused by Mycobacterium abscessus, a group of environmental mycobacteria also found in water, soil, and dust. This organism can also lead to infections in humans. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is actively involved in tracking NTM infections through the Emerging Infections Program. The CDC collaborates with health departments, federal agencies, healthcare providers, and patients to prevent and manage NTM infections.
